prompt: A supermarket chain plans a survey of its loyalty-card members. Put the steps of its sampling design in order.

steps.text: Define the members to be studied: loyalty-card holders in the province who shopped at least once in the past six months.
steps.explanation: The target population comes first: its elements, geographical boundaries and time period.

steps.text: Obtain the loyalty-card database as the list from which respondents will be drawn.
steps.explanation: The sampling frame is the list or procedure from which the sample is drawn, so it follows the definition of the population.

steps.text: Decide to draw members at random from each store region.
steps.explanation: With the frame in hand, the researcher selects a sampling technique.

steps.text: Decide how many members to invite.
steps.explanation: The sample size is determined after the technique.

steps.text: Draw the members, send the invitations, and record how the draw was carried out.
steps.explanation: Finally, the sampling process is executed and documented.

prompt: Each case describes a gap between a survey result and the true population value. Name its source.

cases.text: A survey of a city's residents draws its sample from a directory of landline numbers, which omits most households under 35.
cases.explanation: The list from which the sample is drawn does not correspond to the target population of all residents.

cases.text: Two random samples of 200 customers, drawn from the same complete list in the same week, estimate satisfaction at 71% and 66%.
cases.explanation: Each sample observes only a subset of the population, so their results differ from each other and from the true value. A larger sample would reduce this gap.

cases.text: Respondents asked how many times they ate at a restaurant in the past year report far more visits than the restaurants' receipts show.
cases.explanation: The respondents give inaccurate answers because of faulty recall.

cases.text: In a survey about time use, the busiest people were least likely to reply, so the results understate how busy the population is.
cases.explanation: The people who responded differ systematically from those who did not.

cases.text: A firm doubles the sample drawn from its list of app users to represent all customers, but its estimate does not move closer to the true value.
cases.explanation: Increasing the sample size does not reduce nonsampling error: the list of app users still does not correspond to all customers.

prompt: Match each research situation with the sampling technique appropriate to it.

pairs.term: A manufacturer needs an estimate of the number of households in the country that own an electric bicycle, with a stated margin of error.
pairs.explanation: The finding must be projected to the population with a known level of precision.

pairs.term: A researcher wants ten people to try a draft questionnaire this afternoon before it is finalised.
pairs.explanation: Pretesting does not require projection to the population, so a faster and less expensive sample is appropriate.

pairs.term: A bank needs accurate satisfaction estimates for each of its three account tiers, whose customers differ substantially.
pairs.explanation: The subgroups differ substantially and each must be estimated accurately.

pairs.term: A study requires in-person interviews with farmers spread across hundreds of villages.
pairs.explanation: The population is geographically dispersed and in-person data collection is required, so villages can serve as clusters.

pairs.term: A study targets collectors of vintage mechanical watches, who meet at a small number of clubs and fairs.
pairs.explanation: The population is rare and its members know one another, so initial respondents can identify further ones.

question_text: A survey of 385 customers estimates a proportion with a margin of error of plus or minus five percentage points at 95 percent confidence. The marketing director asks for a margin of plus or minus 2.5 points, at the same confidence level. Approximately how many completed questionnaires are required?
hint: Consider what happens to the sample size when the margin of error is halved.

options.option_explanation: The margin of error appears squared in the formula, so halving it requires more than twice the sample.

options.option_text: About 545, since the margin of error falls with the square root of the sample size.
options.option_explanation: That calculation increases the sample by the square root of two, which reduces the margin only to about 3.5 points.

options.option_text: About 1,540, four times the original sample.
options.option_explanation: Correct. Halving the margin of error requires approximately four times the sample size: 1.96² × 0.25 / 0.025² ≈ 1,537.

options.option_text: It depends on the number of customers the firm has, which the question does not give.
options.option_explanation: For large populations, the required sample size depends on the desired precision, not on the size of the population.

prompt: Each case describes a respondent in an online survey. Name the check that would identify them.

cases.text: A respondent finishes a 15-minute questionnaire in 90 seconds.
cases.explanation: Completion far below the minimum threshold shows that the questions could not have been read.

cases.text: A respondent reports never having flown and then rates the in-flight meals of three airlines.
cases.explanation: The answers to related questions contradict one another.

cases.text: An item reads “For this item, select ‘strongly agree’,” and a respondent selects “neither agree nor disagree,” as on every other item.
cases.explanation: The respondent failed an instruction to select a specific answer.

cases.text: Six completed questionnaires with different names arrive from the same device within ten minutes.
cases.explanation: Technical checks identify duplicate responses from the same device.

cases.text: Asked why they chose their current mobile carrier, a respondent writes a polished paragraph on the general benefits of customer service that names no carrier.
cases.explanation: Generic text that could answer any question, possibly generated by AI, is found by reviewing the open-ended answers.

question_text: A vendor's synthetic panel of 5,000 respondents rates a proposed plant-based cheese at 5.1 on a 7-point purchase-intention scale, with a standard deviation of 0.4, and reports a margin of error of ±0.01. What is the most serious problem with this result?
hint: Consider what connects a sample to the population it describes.

options.option_text: The panel is too small; 10,000 synthetic respondents would reduce the margin of error further.
options.option_explanation: Adding synthetic respondents does not connect them to the population, so the margin of error remains meaningless at any size.

options.option_text: No sampling frame connects the synthetic respondents to the population, so the margin of error cannot be meaningfully calculated, and a new product lies outside the model's experience.
options.option_explanation: Correct. The responses reflect the model's training data, the margin of error has no meaning for a synthetic sample, and the model has no experience of a product absent from that data.

options.option_text: A standard deviation of 0.4 shows that consumers agree closely, which makes the estimate especially reliable.
options.option_explanation: Synthetic responses typically show less variation than real responses, which understates the diversity of opinion rather than demonstrating agreement.

options.option_text: Purchase intention should be measured on a 5-point scale.
options.option_explanation: The number of scale categories is not the problem; the source of the responses is.
